nodes.question: What factors influence the distribution and survival of samphire species?
nodes.answer: The distribution and survival of samphire species are influenced by fluctuations in salinity, water availability, and temperature, with their tolerance to extreme conditions determining their survival.

Turner2 Grant Palmer1 Singarayer Florentine1,3 Received: 22 December 2023 / Revised: 17 January 2025 / Accepted: 10 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Australia is home to a rich assemblage of samphires (Tecticornia and Salicornia spp.) which are largely endemic, inhabiting saline and semi-saline areas across climatically diverse regions. While these plants are adapted to harsh conditions, they are vulnerable to the effects of climate change which is anticipated to exacerbate existing management and environmental pressures. Despite the threatened and priority status of many samphires, there is an overall lack of knowledge surrounding their distribution, ecology and responses to environmental threats, data which we believe is critical to support their conservation and management. We have compiled and critically assessed peer-reviewed and online grey lit- erature and databases to provide an overview of threatened and poorly known samphires in Australia, with particular reference to their distribution, threats and ecological responses.

nodes.question: What factors influence the distribution and survival of samphires in Australia?
nodes.answer: The distribution and survival of samphires are influenced by fluctuations in salinity, water availability, and temperature, with their tolerances to extreme conditions determining their success in harsh environments.
nodes.paragraph: Of the 58 species and 19 subspecies recorded in Australia, two are federally listed as threatened, eight have a formal conservation listing in at least one state or territory, and 25 are recognised as data deficient or priority taxa. Five samphire communities are also listed as threatened and seven are considered Priority Ecological Communities. We found gaps in data relevant to these threatened and priority species, with 40% having fewer than 20 distribution records available nationally. Species were distributed across 11 Conserva- tion Management Zones (and 27 biogeographic regions). Despite their legislative protec- tion, few species have management or recovery plans or peer reviewed ecological studies to guide conservation and management efforts. We propose further research to support effec- tive management of these unique species and ecological communities. Keywords Conservation Halophytes Samphires Tecticornia sp. Salicornia sp. Additionally, many species are yet to be formally evaluated against the Interna- tional Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List threat categories, despite likely meeting the criteria (Le Breton et al. 2019). The number of data-deficient plant spe- cies is also increasing in some regions with the discovery of new, yet undescribed taxa, adding to the backlog of species with inadequate data to assess their conservation status (Gosper et al. 2022). To prevent further decline, it is essential to identify species most at threat or considered poorly known, and gather data to underpin management and conser - vation efforts. Whilst samphire species (Tecticornia Hook.f. and Salicornia L. spp. : Sali- cornioideae Ulbr. : Chenopodiaceae/Amaranthaceae clade) are widespread globally, Aus- tralian species are largely endemic and little is known about most of them. Although many are recognised as threatened, priority or data-deficient, few have specific management plans to assist with their conservation. Samphires are stem-succulent, halophytic plants that occur across a range of saline and semi-saline habitats, from coastal saltmarshes in varied climates to inland salt lakes and saline flats within rangelands of arid and semi-arid regions (Department of the Envi- ronment and Energy [DEE] 2017).

nodes.paragraph: There is greater intensity and frequency of drought, flooding, heat stress and wind, exacerbating existing land management issues (IPCC 2022) such as water extraction, secondary salinisation, habitat fragmentation and mining that threaten the integrity of salt lake ecosystems (Williams 2002; Heydari & Jabbari 2012). Exogenous environmental stressors such as extreme temperatures can impose thresholds for essential ecological functions such as seed germination (Cochrane 2020). The effects of these stress- ors are uncertain in the face of climate change, particularly for species already under threat or with restricted distributions (Elliott et al. 2019; Cochrane 2020), or those with specific environmental requirements (Broadhurst & Coates 2017). Adding to the complexity is that while suitable habitats may contract for some samphire species with climate change (Cole- man 2024), new habitats may become available for other halophytes with the expansion of saline and arid lands. Therefore, it remains important to identify and protect species most at risk of changing conditions. nodes.question: What environmental conditions characterize the study area around the Ebro Delta?
nodes.answer: The area is characterized by strong seasonality, high nutrient availability due to riverine inputs and upwelling events, and a wide continental shelf.

Materials and methods Study area The study area is the surroundings of the Ebro Delta, in the Northwestern Mediterranean Sea, from Vilanova i la Geltr , in the north, to Castell de la Plana, in the south, covering approximately 8,0 km2 and including part of the coastal area, continental shelf, and upper slope (35 400 m) (Fig. 1). Despite that the Mediterranean Sea is generally considered oligotrophic, this area receives high riverine inputs from the Ebro river (Estrada 1996) and from the Rhone River in the north (France), which are transported southwestwards along the continental slope by the Liguro-Proven al-Catalan cur - rent (Estrada 1996). In addition, local upwelling events (i.e., eddies) also enhance nutrient availability. The area is also characterized by strong seasonality (Vilas et al. 2020; Lloret- Lloret et al. 2021). Overall, the wide continental shelf sur - rounding the Ebro Delta, combined with high nutrient avail- ability, upwelling events, and seasonal dynamics, contributes to create a favourable environment for fish nursery for many demersal and pelagic species that also supports high biodi- versity and high biomass, including species of commercial interest (Palomera et al.

nodes.question: What types of species benefit from the environmental conditions in the Ebro Delta?
nodes.answer: The favorable environment supports a variety of fish nursery species, including many demersal and pelagic species, which contribute to high biodiversity and biomass.
